source_text: CAPUT QUARTUM, De statibus Christi. STATUS Christi, qui circa impositionem & executionem horum officiorum ad hoc requisiti sunt, ut nomen Salvatoris secundum voluntatem Patris sui gerere possit, duo sunt: HUMILIATIONIS videlicet & EXALTATIONIS. II. Ad statum humiliationis pertinent passio, crucifixio, mors, sepultura, descensus ad inferos.
english: CHAPTER FOUR. On the states of Christ.

The states of Christ that were required around the imposition and execution of these offices, so that He might bear the name Savior according to the will of His Father, are two: namely of humiliation and of exaltation.
II. To the state of humiliation belong the passion, crucifixion, death, burial, and descent to the lower regions.

source_text: III. PASSIO Christi completur omnis generis contumeliis & cruciatibus tum animae tum corporis, quos partim furor hostium ei intulit, partim immediata Patris castigatio. Initium vero passionum istarum ducimus a captivitate ipsius. Quae enim ipsi antea evenereunt, propassiones potius fuisse existimamus, quam passiones, quibus exploraretur, an etiam malorum ferendorum praescius, & quidem per experimentalem scientiam, nihilominus tamen paratus foret voluntaria obedientia ad ferendum alia. Unde Augustinus: Non, inquit, mortuus est Christus ex necessitate, quia omnipotens, neque ex debito, quia sanctus & immaculatus, sed ex libera voluntate, quia misericors & miserator Dominus. IV. CRUCIFIXIO est modus occisionis, qui docet Christum pro nobis factum esse maledictionem, ut nos per illius crucem a maledictione legis liberaremur. De modo crucifixionis vide praeter alios Justum Lipsium. Crux fuit non execrationis causa, sed tropaeum & signum, ut ex Eusebio Pamphilo & Chrysostomo docet Sanfordus lib. 3 de descensu ad inferos sect. 125.
english: III. The passion of Christ is completed by insults and torments of every kind, both of soul and of body, which partly the fury of enemies inflicted on Him, and partly the immediate chastisement of the Father.

We take the beginning of those sufferings from His captivity. What happened to Him before that we judge to have been foresufferings rather than the sufferings proper, by which it would be tried whether, already foreknowing the evils to be borne, and indeed by experimental knowledge, He would nevertheless be ready by voluntary obedience to bear others still. Hence Augustine: Christ did not die from necessity, because He is omnipotent, nor from debt, because He is holy and immaculate, but from free will, because He is a merciful and compassionate Lord.

IV. Crucifixion is a mode of killing that teaches that Christ was made a curse for us, so that we might be freed by His cross from the curse of the law. On the mode of crucifixion see, among others, Justus Lipsius. The cross was not for the sake of execration, but a trophy and sign, as Sanford teaches from Eusebius Pamphilus and Chrysostom (On the Descent to Hell, book 3, section 125).

source_text: V. MORS Christi est vera animae ipsius a corpore separatio. Hinc Judaei recte dicuntur eum interfecisse, Act. 3:14. VI. SEPULTURA Christi est certa mortis illius confirmatio. VII. DESCENSUS illius ad inferos est status illius a tempore sepulturae usque ad resurrectionem, in quo sub dominio mortis fuisse judicatus est. Fuit autem hic status apprime necessarius, tum ut Patri suo obedientiam praestaret, tum ut tentatus in omnibus, sine peccato tamen, compati posset iis qui tentantur, tum denique ut per passiones in sacerdotem & regem consecraretur, atque ita in gloriam regni sui intraret. Vide Sanfordum & Parkerum libris eruditissimis de descensu ad inferos.
english: V. The death of Christ is the true separation of His soul from the body. Hence the Jews are rightly said to have killed Him (Acts 3:14).
VI. The burial of Christ is a sure confirmation of that death.

VII. His descent to the lower regions is His state from the time of burial until the resurrection, in which He is judged to have been under the dominion of death. This state was especially necessary, both that He might render obedience to His Father, and that, tempted in all things yet without sin, He might be able to sympathize with those who are tempted, and finally that through sufferings He might be consecrated as priest and king, and so enter into the glory of His kingdom. See Sanford and Parker in their most learned books on the descent to hell.

source_text: VIII. Status vero exaltationis complectitur tres potissimum gradus: resurrectionem, ascensionem in caelos, & sessionem ad dextram Dei Patris. IX. RESURRECTIO est initium gloriae & liberatio a vinculis inferni et mortis, qua corpus Christi mortuum inque sepulchro positum, sublatis mortis in eo effectibus, animae suae reunium, & eo in vita, non hanc animalem, sed spiritualem, revocatum est. Etsi tamen & vi abundante animalis vitae munia obire potuerit, quamdiu post resurrectionem in hac vita cum discipulis ad fidem resurrectioni conciliandam commoratus fuerit. Hanc vero resurrectionem non tantum Patri per Spiritum S. verum etiam Christo ipsi, tanquam causae efficienti, tribuimus, quippe qui potestatem habuerit ut ponendi, ita & animam suam resumendi, Joh. 10:17-18. X. ASCENSIO Christi in caelum est exaltationis ipsius progressus, quo cum in terra munus iniunctum administrasset, corpore suo glorioso, ad alia munia saluti hominum procuranda necessaria in caelo ac de caelo obeunda, eo evectionus est, ibidemque permanet, donec ad iudicium reveniat. Ex hoc fonte hauriuntur quaedam solutiones sophismatum, quibus Pontifices quidam dogma de transsubstantiatione, & quidam dogma de consubstantiatione, sive praesentia corporis Christi IN, cum, & SUB pane per indistantiam substantialem defendere videntur, quem errorem tamen sapientiores ut absurdum hodie non agnoscunt.
english: VIII. The state of exaltation embraces three principal degrees: resurrection, ascension into the heavens, and session at the right hand of God the Father.

IX. Resurrection is the beginning of glory and liberation from the bonds of hell and death, by which the dead body of Christ, placed in the tomb, with the effects of death in it removed, was reunited to His soul and recalled into life — not this animal life, but a spiritual one. Yet by an overflowing power He could also discharge the offices of animal life for as long as after the resurrection He remained in this life with the disciples to win faith for the resurrection. We attribute this resurrection not only to the Father through the Holy Spirit, but also to Christ Himself as efficient cause, since He had power both to lay down and to take up again His soul (John 10:17-18).

X. The ascension of Christ into heaven is the progress of His exaltation, by which, after He had administered on earth the office enjoined on Him, He was taken up in His glorious body to discharge in heaven and from heaven other offices necessary for procuring the salvation of men, and there He remains until He returns for judgment. From this fountain are drawn certain solutions of the sophisms by which some papal writers seem to defend the dogma of transubstantiation, and some the dogma of consubstantiation, or of the presence of Christ's body IN, with, and UNDER the bread by substantial non-distance — an error that wiser men today do not acknowledge, as absurd.

source_text: XI. SESSIO Christi ad dextram Patris est supremus gradus exaltationis illius, quo summa gloria & potestas regia cum pleno imperio in caelo & in terra super omnia & in omnia creata, & dignitas fungendi porro muneris sacerdotalis in ista actione, quae in caelis a sacerdote caelis facto sublimiore peragenda erat, Christo ipsi a Patre communicata continetur. Est autem hic status exaltationis duabus potissimum de causis necessarius: 1. Propter officium sacerdotale, quia debuit in caelo coram Patris facie comparere sanguine suo aspersus, & intercedere pro fidelibus. 2. Propter munus regium, quia debuit de caelis verbum (ubi prophetiae administratio regio muneri subordinata intelligitur) & Spiritum mittere, omnia in novitu obsignata conferendo obtemperantibus ipsi, mala vero infligendo immorigeris, postquam hi Dei patientia abusi fuerint, quam iustitia eius tolerare potuit. Et huius administrationis actus erit iudicium universale, quod exspectamus, & explicavimus lib. 2 c. 13. CAPUT QUINTUM sequitur, De satisfactione Christi.
english: XI. The session of Christ at the right hand of the Father is the supreme degree of that exaltation, which contains the highest glory and kingly power with full empire in heaven and on earth over all and in all created things, and the dignity of further discharging the priestly office in that action which was to be carried out in the heavens by the priest made higher than the heavens — all communicated to Christ Himself by the Father.

This state of exaltation is necessary especially for two reasons: 1. Because of the priestly office, since He had to appear in heaven before the Father's face, sprinkled with His own blood, and intercede for the faithful. 2. Because of the kingly munus, since He had to send from the heavens the Word (where the administration of prophecy is understood as subordinated to the kingly munus) and the Spirit, conferring all things sealed in the New Testament on those who obey Him, but inflicting evils on the disobedient after they have abused the patience of God, which His justice could tolerate. And the act of this administration will be the universal judgment that we await, and that we explained in Book II, chapter 13.
CHAPTER FIVE follows, On the satisfaction of Christ.
